content_html:
In M. John Harrison’s​ short story ‘The Crisis’, first published in 2017, the world has been invaded by aliens that look like ‘stalks of fleshy, weak rhubarb’. Except they might not be aliens; it might not be an invasion. Nobody’s quite sure what they are, or where they’ve come from, or whether they’re even ‘here’ in the conventional sense. They gravitate towards the City of London, transforming it into a spectral no-go zone. ‘You would see them for a fraction of a second just at the city skyline behind the buildings, just under the cloudbase, evolving very fast like stop-frame film of something organic growing, then running out of energy, then growing again.’ Some people associate them with dark matter. Others think they’ve emerged ‘out of the internet’. They become known as the iGhetti, for some reason. Attempts to combat them are futile. ‘The sirens would go off, all across the city from Borough to Camden. The artillery would fire and recoil, fire and recoil. The iGhetti would pulse and grow against the lighted clouds.’ It’s hard to maintain a sense of emergency. Displaced finance workers go home to their Georgian terraces and occupy themselves collecting modern first editions or doing triathlons. In places as close to the front line as Liverpool Street and the Barbican, restaurants, cafés and art galleries remain open. ‘It was as if nothing had changed, as if the City fringe, like West London, still believed itself to be intact, functioning, the heart of what we used to call, before money lost its confidence, an “economy”.’

An atmosphere of collective denial – of a society adapting to disaster by learning to ignore it – is even stronger in The End of Everything. Harrison’s new novel is a return to the scenario of ‘The Crisis’, but the iGhetti are now more firmly established (a reference to Covid in a character’s childhood seems to place the action in the 2040s), and though they’re still focused on the Square Mile, the setting is the stretch of semi-gentrified, semi-bohemian coastal towns between Hastings and Margate. On one level, everything is painted in familiarly dystopian colours. Acts of sudden, extreme violence have become routine, and law enforcement is a matter for vigilante bands. Air travel and news media are things of the past. Refugees pile onto boats bound for Europe, ‘the lost continent’, but ‘no one ever comes back from there to say whether they found it or not.’ Yet all along the seafront, waiters serve coffee and croissants to weekenders watching the sunrise. Around midday, retirees emerge from their mansion flats to have amiable arguments about Henry VIII and the Battle of Britain. At night, music blares out of neon-fronted bars. Nobody makes much effort to understand or even acknowledge the changes that have occurred. ‘It had been a long time since anyone could make sense of anything.’

Phillip Tennent, the novel’s unsatisfied, ineffectual hero, came here from London in his early twenties, less in the hope of putting distance between himself and the iGhetti than because he was drawn by ‘some internal compass of nostalgia’ towards his aunt Marnie, a painter who arrived ‘a generation ago’, when the town was still ‘a thriving arts community’. Now Tennent is 38 and eking out a living as a beachcomber, while Marnie is 70, ‘lively and determined one minute, precarious the next’. They’re no longer close, but in the opening pages Tennent shows up at Marnie’s house with something he’s found in the sea. More or less human in appearance, it’s actually ‘hybrid technology, some kind of biological gadget the iGhetti had released in numbers when they first arrived, which was no longer of use to them’. It’s about the size of a baby, but growing fast. At first it speaks exclusively in gnomic phrases (‘I don’t want to see it, I just want to be it’ or ‘a new life … is beginning’), but by the end of the novel it has learned to read and can reel off various esoteric facts, though there’s no way of checking them. Tennent and Marnie don’t bother to give it a name. It’s referred to throughout as ‘the artefact’, ‘the object’ or ‘the item’. The plot – if that’s the right word for such a fragile, open-ended structure – largely revolves around their efforts to get rid of it.

On his blog, Harrison describes The End of Everything as his attempt to write a novel ‘that might have been submitted for serialisation in New Worlds in 1967’. That makes it sound like a throwback – a curious project for a writer of science fiction. Apart from the odd mannerism – the male characters are called by their last names and the female ones by their first – it doesn’t feel especially retro, but perhaps Harrison has in mind an attitude rather than a technique.

New Worlds sought to transform science fiction from a species of adolescent escapism into a branch of the avant-garde. In 1967 the magazine published countercultural classics including Thomas M. Disch’s Camp Concentration (in which draft dodgers are subjected to sinister medical experiments) and J.G. Ballard’s ‘Notes towards a Mental Breakdown’ (which features the Apollo 1 astronauts and an obsessive restaging of the Kennedy assassination). The following year, aged 23, Harrison joined its editorial staff; he ran the books pages until it ceased regular publication in 1976. The dozens of essays and reviews he wrote during his tenure (many of them published under the name Joyce Churchill) trace the formation of a distinct aesthetic. He came to feel that mainstream science fiction wasn’t just inane: in its indifference to ordinary experience it was reprehensible. As he put it in a 1975 essay, ‘at times there can be sensed at the hub of the genre something so repellent, so intolerably fixated and vacuous that you don’t know quite whether to choke or laugh.’

Since his New Worlds period, Harrison hasn’t limited himself to science fiction. The semi-autobiographical Climbers (1989), set in the Peak District, became the first novel to receive the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature. The Course of the Heart (1992), about a group of Cambridge students dabbling in the occult, was a formative influence on the loosely defined fantasy/horror movement known as the New Weird (it was Harrison who gave it the name, in an introduction to China Miéville’s 2002 novella The Tain). But whether the setting is West Yorkshire in the 1980s or a semi-sentient spaceship in 2400, his determination to say something about ordinary experience – specifically, the experience of feeling rudderless and dazed – has been unwavering. In his ‘anti-memoir’, Wish I Was Here (2023), he sets out his credo:

Massive amounts of what happens to you will happen via invisible and/or unparsable causal chains. Much of life, you will never know what happens to you at all, let alone to anyone else. Much of what goes on around you, you will never even notice. Though causes are everywhere present and dependable, the search for causality is to welter around looking for explanations you can’t have, using epistemologies and ontologies at best provisional. Why waste time, especially in fiction? Let’s have some representation in fiction for everyone who, without knowing it, puzzles through their lives in what used to be called ‘a dream’ … I’m not sure life is a dream. But if your attempts to map it don’t feel like one, you may be making a serious error about what being awake actually is, or where and in what conditions it is carried out.

Harrison’s novels enact dreamy puzzling-through at every level. They dispense with much of the usual narrative infrastructure: linear plotting, legible motive, dramatic resolution. The dialogue is scrappy and oblique. The central characters are baffled underachievers, spiritually enervated men and women whose personal crises distract them from the crisis facing the species. The hero of The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again (2020) is typical:

During his fifties Shaw went through a rough patch. That was how he put it to himself. His adult life had been, until then, perfectly normal. He had been determined on normality. Perhaps that had been the problem. Anyway, his life lost shape and five years were expended on nothing very much. They slid into themselves like the parts of a trick box and wouldn’t open again. He would wake up to himself with utter clarity in – say – a crowded first-floor noodle bar at night, talking to people he didn’t know while he looked down into a street full of brand-new motorcycles. Then everything would slip away again, to be lived at one remove for a week or two.

In The End of Everything, ‘bad patches’ are external features of the landscape. They have something to do with the crisis, though it’s not clear whether they’re ‘a weapon in themselves’ or simply ‘a side issue of the iGhetti’s way of existing’. At times they’re static phenomena that cause epic hallucinations; at others they’re ‘smaller, unanchored events’ that drift around ‘like fogs or showers of rain’ and trigger nothing worse than light-headedness and a rush of false memories. One result of all this is that it’s hard to be confident that anything’s real. At one point, Marnie enters a bad patch in which she sees a strange vehicle speeding towards her from a roundabout. It’s described across four short chapters, each of which is titled ‘The Sign’: this mild formal breach is the only indication that the episode isn’t of a piece with all the other weird stuff in the book.

Novels in which the characters don’t understand what’s happening are hardly rare, but mystification is both Harrison’s subject and his method. It’s an approach that throws up some obvious technical problems. How to frustrate understanding without sacrificing interest? His solution is to be explicit about psychological and emotional matters while remaining vague about everything else. For a writer bent on capturing equivocal moods, he can be surprisingly fond of direct statement. He’s quite capable of conveying ambiguity by saying ‘there was a vigorous ambiguity to everything,’ or of evoking terror with the words ‘a sense of terror overcame her.’ Adjectives like ‘puzzled’, ‘confused’, ‘unsure’, ‘uncertain’ and ‘befuddled’ get a lot of exercise. At his best, though, his deranged images and impeccably glazed sentences create a powerful sense of puzzlement or terror without his having to spell it out. This effect is at its strongest when it comes to the artefact, which by the end of the novel is ‘the size of an adult human being’ but still has ‘an unformed look’ and ‘a shy, inturned smile’. At times it seems like a person, at others like an alien, at others like AI. At one point, frightened by a fire, it runs around ‘like a long dog’. It’s an uncanny little blighter, whatever it is. In the final section, it embarks on a road trip with Marnie, who begins to think of it as ‘the driver’:

She sat cocooned in the warmth of the car while the road rushed past and the driver told her about the stars. Its overwhelmingly boyish enthusiasms often made her think. Now she stared at its profile in the blue light of the dashboard … and saw once again that it was an artefact from the sea. No one knew what those things were supposed to do, or how they viewed a real person like her.

‘What’s the point of an alien artefact you can recognise?’ Harrison asked in Wish I Was Here. ‘As a branch of the fantastic, science fiction should accept that its currency is the inexplicable, not the explicable.’ That principle could hardly be taken much further than it is in The End of Everything. There’s little point in trying to make it all add up. The iGhetti are both here and not here. The world is ending and it isn’t. It’s 2040-something; it’s 2026; it’s still 1967.

blocks.html_en: Phillip Tennent, the novel’s unsatisfied, ineffectual hero, came here from London in his early twenties, less in the hope of putting distance between himself and the iGhetti than because he was drawn by ‘some internal compass of nostalgia’ towards his aunt Marnie, a painter who arrived ‘a generation ago’, when the town was still ‘a thriving arts community’. Now Tennent is 38 and eking out a living as a beachcomber, while Marnie is 70, ‘lively and determined one minute, precarious the next’. They’re no longer close, but in the opening pages Tennent shows up at Marnie’s house with something he’s found in the sea. More or less human in appearance, it’s actually ‘hybrid technology, some kind of biological gadget the iGhetti had released in numbers when they first arrived, which was no longer of use to them’. It’s about the size of a baby, but growing fast. At first it speaks exclusively in gnomic phrases (‘I don’t want to see it, I just want to be it’ or ‘a new life … is beginning’), but by the end of the novel it has learned to read and can reel off various esoteric facts, though there’s no way of checking them. Tennent and Marnie don’t bother to give it a name. It’s referred to throughout as ‘the artefact’, ‘the object’ or ‘the item’. The plot – if that’s the right word for such a fragile, open-ended structure – largely revolves around their efforts to get rid of it.

blocks.html_en: New Worlds sought to transform science fiction from a species of adolescent escapism into a branch of the avant-garde. In 1967 the magazine published countercultural classics including Thomas M. Disch’s Camp Concentration (in which draft dodgers are subjected to sinister medical experiments) and J.G. Ballard’s ‘Notes towards a Mental Breakdown’ (which features the Apollo 1 astronauts and an obsessive restaging of the Kennedy assassination). The following year, aged 23, Harrison joined its editorial staff; he ran the books pages until it ceased regular publication in 1976. The dozens of essays and reviews he wrote during his tenure (many of them published under the name Joyce Churchill) trace the formation of a distinct aesthetic. He came to feel that mainstream science fiction wasn’t just inane: in its indifference to ordinary experience it was reprehensible. As he put it in a 1975 essay, ‘at times there can be sensed at the hub of the genre something so repellent, so intolerably fixated and vacuous that you don’t know quite whether to choke or laugh.’

blocks.html_en: Since his New Worlds period, Harrison hasn’t limited himself to science fiction. The semi-autobiographical Climbers (1989), set in the Peak District, became the first novel to receive the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature. The Course of the Heart (1992), about a group of Cambridge students dabbling in the occult, was a formative influence on the loosely defined fantasy/horror movement known as the New Weird (it was Harrison who gave it the name, in an introduction to China Miéville’s 2002 novella The Tain). blocks.html_en: Massive amounts of what happens to you will happen via invisible and/or unparsable causal chains. Much of life, you will never know what happens to you at all, let alone to anyone else. Much of what goes on around you, you will never even notice. Though causes are everywhere present and dependable, the search for causality is to welter around looking for explanations you can’t have, using epistemologies and ontologies at best provisional. Why waste time, especially in fiction? Let’s have some representation in fiction for everyone who, without knowing it, puzzles through their lives in what used to be called ‘a dream’ … I’m not sure life is a dream. But if your attempts to map it don’t feel like one, you may be making a serious error about what being awake actually is, or where and in what conditions it is carried out.

blocks.html_en: In The End of Everything, ‘bad patches’ are external features of the landscape. They have something to do with the crisis, though it’s not clear whether they’re ‘a weapon in themselves’ or simply ‘a side issue of the iGhetti’s way of existing’. At times they’re static phenomena that cause epic hallucinations; at others they’re ‘smaller, unanchored events’ that drift around ‘like fogs or showers of rain’ and trigger nothing worse than light-headedness and a rush of false memories. One result of all this is that it’s hard to be confident that anything’s real. At one point, Marnie enters a bad patch in which she sees a strange vehicle speeding towards her from a roundabout. It’s described across four short chapters, each of which is titled ‘The Sign’: this mild formal breach is the only indication that the episode isn’t of a piece with all the other weird stuff in the book.

blocks.html_en: Novels in which the characters don’t understand what’s happening are hardly rare, but mystification is both Harrison’s subject and his method. It’s an approach that throws up some obvious technical problems. How to frustrate understanding without sacrificing interest? His solution is to be explicit about psychological and emotional matters while remaining vague about everything else. For a writer bent on capturing equivocal moods, he can be surprisingly fond of direct statement. He’s quite capable of conveying ambiguity by saying ‘there was a vigorous ambiguity to everything,’ or of evoking terror with the words ‘a sense of terror overcame her.’ Adjectives like ‘puzzled’, ‘confused’, ‘unsure’, ‘uncertain’ and ‘befuddled’ get a lot of exercise. At his best, though, his deranged images and impeccably glazed sentences create a powerful sense of puzzlement or terror without his having to spell it out. This effect is at its strongest when it comes to the artefact, which by the end of the novel is ‘the size of an adult human being’ but still has ‘an unformed look’ and ‘a shy, inturned smile’. At times it seems like a person, at others like an alien, at others like AI. At one point, frightened by a fire, it runs around ‘like a long dog’. It’s an uncanny little blighter, whatever it is. content_html_zh:
在M。 约翰·哈里森的短篇小说《危机》于 2017 年首次出版，世界被看起来像“肉质、弱大黄的茎”的外星人入侵。 但他们可能不是外星人；这可能不是入侵。 没有人确切知道它们是什么，或者它们来自哪里，或者它们是否在传统意义上的“这里”。 他们倾向于伦敦金融城，将其变成一个幽灵禁区。 “你会在建筑物后面的城市天际线、云底下的几分之一秒内看到它们，它们的演变速度非常快，就像有机物生长的定格胶片一样，然后耗尽能量，然后再次生长。” 有些人将它们与暗物质联系起来。 其他人则认为他们是“从互联网中脱颖而出”的。 由于某种原因，他们被称为 iGhetti。 与他们作斗争的尝试是徒劳的。 “从自治市镇到卡姆登，整个城市的警报都会响起。 火炮会开火、后坐、开火、后坐。 iGhetti 会在明亮的云层中跳动并生长。 保持紧迫感是很困难的。 流离失所的金融工作者回到格鲁吉亚露台的家中，忙着收集现代初版或参加铁人三项比赛。 在利物浦街和巴比肯等靠近前线的地方，餐馆、咖啡馆和艺术画廊仍然开放。 “就好像什么都没有改变，好像伦敦金融城的边缘地带，就像西伦敦一样，仍然相信自己完好无损、运转良好，是在金钱失去信心之前我们所说的‘经济’的核心。”

集体否认的氛围——社会通过学会忽视灾难来适应灾难——在《一切的终结》中更加强烈。 哈里森的新小说回归了《危机》的场景，但 iGhetti 现在已经更加牢固地确立了（在角色童年时提到新冠疫情似乎将故事情节设定在 2040 年代），尽管他们的重点仍然是“一平方英里”，但背景却是黑斯廷斯和马盖特之间的一片半中产阶级化、半波西米亚风格的沿海城镇。 一方面，一切都被描绘成熟悉的反乌托邦色彩。 突然、极端的暴力行为已成为家常便饭，而执法则是治安维持队的职责。 航空旅行和新闻媒体已成为过去。 难民涌上开往欧洲“失落的大陆”的船只，但“没有人从那里回来说他们是否找到了它。” 然而，在海滨，服务员为周末观看日出的人们提供咖啡和羊角面包。 中午时分，退休人员从他们的豪宅公寓出来，就亨利八世和不列颠之战进行友好的争论。 晚上，霓虹灯饰的酒吧里传出刺耳的音乐声。 没有人付出太多努力来理解甚至承认已经发生的变化。 “已经很久没有人能够理解任何事情了。”

小说中心怀不满、无能的主人公菲利普·坦南特 (Phillip Tennent) 在二十出头的时候从伦敦来到这里，与其说是希望拉开自己与 iGhetti 之间的距离，不如说是因为他被“某种内心的怀旧之情”所吸引，对他的姨妈玛妮 (Marnie) 产生了兴趣。玛妮是一位画家，“一代人前”来到这里，当时小镇还是“一个繁荣的艺术社区”。 现在坦南特已经 38 岁了，靠海滩流浪勉强维持生计，而玛妮已经 70 岁了，“前一分钟活泼而坚定，下一分钟就岌岌可危”。 他们不再亲密，但在开头几页中，坦南特带着他在海里发现的东西出现在玛妮的家里。 外观或多或少是人类的，它实际上是“混合技术，一种 iGhetti 在他们刚到达时大量释放的生物装置，但对他们来说不再有用了”。 它和婴儿差不多大，但长得很快。 起初，它只用一些格言短语来表达（“我不想看到它，我只想成为它”或“新生活...... 正在开始”），但到了小说的结尾，它已经学会了阅读，并且可以滔滔不绝地讲述各种深奥的事实，尽管没有办法检查它们。 坦南特和玛妮懒得给它起名字。 它在全文中被称为“人工制品”、“物体”或“物品”。 情节——如果这个词适合描述这样一个脆弱的、开放式的结构——主要围绕着他们摆脱它的努力。

哈里森在他的博客上将《一切的终结》描述为他尝试写一部“可能会在 1967 年在《新世界》连载”的小说。 这听起来像是一种倒退——对于科幻小说作家来说，这是一个奇怪的项目。 除了奇怪的举止——男性角色以姓氏称呼，女性角色以名字称呼——它并没有让人感觉特别复古，但也许哈里森想到的是一种态度而不是一种技巧。

新世界试图将科幻小说从一种青少年逃避现实的小说转变为先锋派的一个分支。 1967 年，该杂志出版了反主流文化的经典作品，其中包括 Thomas M. 迪施集中营（避兵者在此接受险恶的医学实验）和 J.G. 巴拉德的《精神崩溃笔记》（以阿波罗 1 号宇航员和对肯尼迪遇刺事件的痴迷重演为特色）。 次年，23 岁的哈里森加入了编辑团队；他负责管理这本书的版面，直到该书于 1976 年停止定期出版。 他在任职期间撰写的数十篇文章和评论（其中许多以乔伊斯·丘吉尔的名义发表）追溯了独特美学的形成。 他开始觉得主流科幻小说不仅是愚蠢的：它对普通经验的漠视是应该受到谴责的。 正如他在 1975 年的一篇文章中所说，“有时可以在这一流派的中心感觉到一些令人厌恶的东西，如此令人难以忍受的固定和空虚，以至于你不知道是该窒息还是大笑。”

自新世界时期以来，哈里森并没有将自己局限于科幻小说。 以峰区为背景的半自传体《登山者》（1989）成为第一部获得博德曼·塔斯克山区文学奖的小说。 《心灵的历程》（The Course of the Heart，1992）讲述了一群剑桥​​学生涉足神秘学的故事，它对被称为“新怪异”的松散定义的奇幻/恐怖运动产生了影响（哈里森在齐纳·米耶维尔 2002 年的中篇小说《泰恩》的介绍中给它起了这个名字）。 但无论背景是 20 世纪 80 年代的西约克郡，还是 2400 年的半智能宇宙飞船，他讲述日常生活经验的决心——特别是那种失去舵手和茫然的经历——都坚定不移。 在他的“反回忆录”《希望我在这里》（2023 年）中，他阐述了自己的信条：

发生在你身上的大量事情将通过不可见和/或不可解析的因果链发生。 在生活的大部分时间里，你永远不会知道发生在你身上的事情，更不用说发生在其他人身上了。 你周围发生的很多事情，你甚至都不会注意到。 尽管原因无处不在且可靠，但对因果关系的探索就是四处寻找你无法找到的解释，最多只能使用临时的认识论和本体论。 为什么要浪费时间，尤其是在小说上？ 让我们在小说中为那些不知不觉地在过去被称为“梦”的生活中困惑的人提供一些描述…… 我不确定生活是不是一场梦。 但如果你尝试绘制它的感觉并不像清醒，那么你可能在清醒的实际含义或清醒的地点和条件方面犯了严重错误。

哈里森的小说在各个层面上演了梦幻般的谜题。 它们摒弃了许多常见的叙事基础设施：线性情节、清晰的动机、戏剧性的解决方案。 对话是杂乱而隐晦的。 中心人物是困惑的后进生、精神衰弱的男人和女人，他们的个人危机分散了他们对物种面临的危机的注意力。 《沉没的土地重新崛起》（2020）的主人公很典型：

五十多岁时，肖经历了一段艰难的时期。 他就是这么对自己说的。 在那之前，他的成年生活一直是完全正常的。 他已经下定决心要保持正常状态。 也许这就是问题所在。 无论如何，他的生活已经失去了意义，五年的时间毫无意义。 它们就像魔术盒的一部分一样滑入自身，再也无法打开。 晚上，他会在一家拥挤的一楼面馆里清醒过来，一边与不认识的人交谈，一边俯视着满是崭新摩托车的街道。 然后一切都会再次溜走，在一个地方生活一两个星期。

在《一切的终结》中，“坏斑块”是景观的外部特征。 它们与这场危机有关，尽管尚不清楚它们是“本身的武器”还是仅仅是“iGhetti 存在方式的一个附带问题”。 有时，它们是静态现象，会引起史诗般的幻觉；有时，它们是静态现象。在另一些人看来，它们是“较小的、无固定的事件”，“像雾气或阵雨”一样四处飘荡，除了引发头晕和虚假记忆之外，没有什么比这更糟糕的了。 所有这一切的结果之一是，很难确信任何事情都是真实的。 有一次，玛妮进入了一个糟糕的地方，她看到一辆奇怪的车辆从环形交叉路口向她驶来。 它通过四个简短的章节进行了描述，每一章的标题都是“标志”：这种轻微的正式违规是唯一表明这一集与书中所有其他奇怪内容不相符的迹象。

小说中的人物不明白正在发生的事情并不罕见，但神秘化既是哈里森的主题，也是他的方法。 这种方法会带来一些明显的技术问题。 如何在不牺牲兴趣的情况下阻碍理解？ 他的解决方案是明确心理和情感问题，同时对其他一切保持模糊。 对于一个致力于捕捉模棱两可情绪的作家来说，他可能会出人意料地喜欢直接陈述。 他很擅长通过说“一切都充满了强烈的模糊性”来表达歧义，或者用“一种恐惧感征服了她”来唤起恐惧。 像“困惑”、“困惑”、“不确定”、“不确定”和“困惑”这样的形容词得到了很多运用。 然而，在他最好的时候，他疯狂的图像和无可挑剔的呆板句子创造了一种强烈的困惑或恐怖感，而无需他把它拼出来。 当涉及到人工制品时，这种效果最为强烈，在小说的结尾，该人工制品“有成年人的大小”，但仍然具有“未成形的外观”和“害羞、内向的微笑”。 有时它看起来像一个人，有时像外星人，有时又像人工智能。 有一次，它被火吓坏了，“像一条长狗”到处乱跑。 不管它是什么，这都是一个不可思议的小祸害。 在最后一部分，它与玛妮一起踏上了公路旅行，玛妮开始将它视为“司机”：

当道路飞驰而过时，她坐在温暖的车里，司机给她讲述星星。 这种孩子气的热情常常让她思考。 现在她在仪表板的蓝光下盯着它的轮廓…… 再次看到那是来自大海的人工制品。 没有人知道这些东西应该做什么，或者他们如何看待像她这样的真实的人。

“你能认出一件外星文物有什么意义？” 哈里森在《希望我在这里》中问道。 “作为奇幻小说的一个分支，科幻小说应该接受这样的事实：它的通行证是无法解释的，而不是无法解释的。” 这一原则几乎不可能比《一切的终结》中的内容走得更远。 试图让这一切加起来没有什么意义。 iGhetti 既在这里又不在这里。 世界正在终结，但事实并非如此。 这是 2040 年左右的事；现在是 2026 年；现在还是1967年。
